title: Portal Preview
tagline: A first look at the Transfer Portal and how internal mobility surfaces.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for all Vanderbilt staff: preview the Transfer Portal, get your skills profile ready for it, and hear it said plainly: moving inside Vanderbilt is a career path the university wants you to take.
heroLead: Until now, finding an internal opportunity meant knowing someone or watching job boards. The Transfer Portal flips that: opportunities across Vanderbilt find you, based on skills and interests you have named. This preview shows you how to be findable.
objectives: Describe what the Transfer Portal does: internal opportunities surfaced to you by skills
Get findable: bring your skills profile current and put your interests in writing
Treat an internal move as a normal, encouraged Vanderbilt career path
missionTie: Defining the great university of the 21st Century takes talent that can flow to where it matters most. Destination Vanderbilt means people choose to come here; the Transfer Portal is how they keep choosing to stay and grow here.
goalLead: Goal 1 promises a system that connects employees to internal opportunities across the university. Today you see it coming, and you get findable before it arrives.

agenda.d: Internal opportunities that surface to you, matched on skills and interests.
The profile and the named interest that let the matching work for you.
Retiring the old myths about applying internally at Vanderbilt.

manifesto: The next opportunity should find you. Make yourself findable.

sections.headline: Opportunities that come looking.
sections.lead: The Transfer Portal is part of Goal 1's talent system, launching this year. You keep a skills profile; the Portal matches it against internal openings, stretch projects, and growth roles across Vanderbilt, and brings the fits to you.
sections.group: In pairs: what would you want the Portal to know about you that your job title never says? One pair shares.
sections.solo: Write down what you would want the Portal to know about you that your job title never says.

card.text: The Portal reads skills and interests, never just titles. A named skill can match a role in a school you have never worked in; a named interest can surface a project before it is ever posted. What it cannot read is anything you left blank.

interaction.q: Quick check: what does the Portal use to surface an opportunity to you?

opts.t: Your current job title and department
opts.why: Titles are the least of it. Two people with the same title can have completely different skills, and the matching runs on the skills.

opts.t: The skills and interests you have named in your profile
opts.why: Exactly. The match runs on what you have declared. That is why the readiness work in the next section matters more than any search technique.
No gatekeeper sits between you and the matching. Managers stay in the loop as coaches and advocates, and the Portal reads your profile directly.

sections.headline: Findable is a choice.
sections.lead: Matching is only as good as what it can read. Two moves make you findable before launch: a skills profile that says what you can actually do, and interests named in writing. Build both here.

interaction.intro: Two entries decide what the Portal can see. Choose how you write your skills and how you name your interest.

opts.t: Copy the duties list from your job description.
opts.coach: The Portal already knows your job exists. Duties describe the role; the matching needs the skills, including the ones your role never uses.

opts.t: List your strongest skills from this role only.
opts.coach: Good start, half the picture. Skills from past roles, volunteer work, and side projects match real openings too. Claim all of it.

opts.t: List every skill you can actually use, from any role, with a line on how you have used it.
opts.coach: Full inventory plus evidence. The how-I-used-it line is what turns a keyword into a credible match.

opts.t: Leave it blank; you don't want to seem restless.
opts.coach: A blank field gives the matching nowhere to aim. Naming an interest signals ambition, and Vanderbilt is asking for exactly that signal.

opts.t: Write something broad like 'open to opportunities.'
opts.coach: Broad interest matches everything, which means it matches nothing well. The Portal can act on 'project work in student-facing units'; it cannot act on 'open.'

opts.t: Name a direction: the kind of work, the skills you want to grow, what you would say yes to.
opts.coach: Specific and forward-looking. This is the entry that surfaces a stretch project before it is posted anywhere.

heads.strong: Findable. Your profile gives the matching real material, and the surfaced fits will look like you on your best day.
heads.mid: Partially visible. The Portal can see the role you have; it still cannot see the person you are.
heads.weak: Invisible. The matching has nothing to read, so the opportunities will keep going to people who wrote things down.

reactions.strong: Weeks after launch, a project in another school surfaces on your dashboard, matched to a skill your current role never uses. It looks interesting. It found you.
reactions.mid: The matches that surface look a lot like your current job in different buildings. Accurate, and underwhelming. The missing half of your profile was the interesting half.
reactions.weak: Launch comes and goes. A colleague with your exact skills gets surfaced for a project you would have loved. The difference between you was a written-down profile.

sections.headline: An internal move is a career path.
sections.lead: The Portal only works if people believe using it is safe. So hear the policy out loud: internal mobility is a normal, encouraged career path at Vanderbilt. Keeping talent inside the university is the point of Goal 1. Some old myths need retiring first.
sections.group: In pairs: what have you heard, in any workplace, about what happens to people who apply internally? Myth or real, 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Write down one thing you have believed about applying internally. After this section, decide: myth or real?

interaction.intro: How people talk about internal moves decides whether anyone makes them. Call each one before the Portal launches into that culture.
interaction.passMsg: You can hear the difference. Retire the myths out loud; they only survive in silence.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The tell: myths punish ambition, normal moves grow careers inside Vanderbilt, and readiness gaps are just profiles waiting to be written.

items.q: 'Don't let your manager see you looking at internal postings. They'll take it personally.'
items.why: This is the myth the Portal is built to kill. A move inside Vanderbilt keeps the talent here, and managers are measured on growing people, never on holding them.

items.q: An advisor sees a program role in another college that fits their skills, tells their manager, and applies.
items.why: This is the path working as designed. The manager conversation is a courtesy and a coaching chance; the application needs nobody's permission.

items.q: A financial analyst wants project work badly, but their profile lists nothing beyond their current job title.
items.why: No myth and no move here, just a matching engine with nothing to read. One honest hour on the profile fixes it.

recap.q: What does the Transfer Portal match on when it surfaces an opportunity?
opts: The skills and interests you have named
recap.why: The matching reads what you have declared. Blank fields match nothing, which is why findability is the readiness work.

recap.q: What makes a skills profile genuinely findable?
opts: A copy of your job description
All your usable skills, any role, with how you used them
Only skills your manager has signed off on
Keeping it short so it is easy to read
recap.why: Full inventory plus evidence, past roles included. The interesting matches usually come from the skills your current job never uses.

recap.q: A colleague applies for an internal role in another school. What is that at Vanderbilt?
opts: A risky move to keep quiet
recap.why: Internal mobility keeps talent inside the university, which is the point of Goal 1. Managers coach the move; they never gate the application.

recapMsgs.high: You are Portal-ready. Now write the profile you built in section two for real.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Take another look at the findability section, then build your card.
recapMsgs.low: Worth a second pass through the three sections before you commit.

capstone.headline: Findable before launch.
capstone.lead: Pick the move that makes you findable. Your own words, your own career; nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: What should the Portal know about you? One skill or interest your title hides.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. process mapping; interested in student-facing project work
capstone.whoRow: The skill or interest to surface

practices.name: The skills sweep
practices.move: Spend one honest hour listing every skill you can actually use, from any role, with one line each on how you have used it.

practices.name: The named interest
practices.move: Write the direction you would say yes to: the kind of work, the skills you want to grow. Then share it with your manager.

practices.name: The internal scan
practices.move: Browse current internal openings once, on purpose, and note one role or project that pulls at you and why.

whens.out: The move happens this week, done by Friday.
You bring it to your next 1:1: here is what I want the Portal to know about me.
The move happens within two weeks, time blocked today so it cannot slide.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what did you claim that your job title never showed?

closing.headline: Be findable. Then be found.
closing.lead: You previewed the Portal, built a findable profile, and retired the old myths. Thursday deepens the same theme with the skill that moves careers fastest: advocacy.
closing.nextTag: Your one next step · This week
closing.nextTitle: Make the findability move on your card
closing.nextBody: Run it as built: one honest hour, one named interest, or one deliberate scan. Curious what makes people stay and grow? This month's LinkedIn Learning pick, Retaining Your Best Talent by Roberta Matuson, comes with a navigator-led stay-interview practice lab.
closing.brandline: Skills written down are skills in play.

facilitator.audience: All Vanderbilt staff in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm; no management experience assumed. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; January is the Retain, Grow, Move month on succession and internal mobility.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did the findability move on your card happen? What did you claim that your title never showed? What direction did you name?' Count of completed findability moves is the Level 3 metric for the month.

s1.title: What the Portal does
s1.purpose: Preview the Transfer Portal plainly: opportunities surfaced to staff by skills and interests, with no gatekeeper in the middle.
s1.say: Here is the honest history of internal opportunity almost everywhere: you found it if you knew somebody or happened to check the right board in the right week. Goal 1 replaces luck with matching. The Transfer Portal reads the skills and interests you have named and brings the fits to you: roles, projects, growth work, across all of Vanderbilt.
facilitate: Read the concept card once; the matching rule is the whole slide.
Run the knowledge check; everyone answers on their own screen.
Run the breakout: what should the Portal know about you that your title never says?

ask.q: What is the first thing you would want the Portal to surface for you?
expect: A next role, said a little shyly
Some have never been asked this before
ask.respond: Every answer just named an interest. Notice how fast they surfaced once someone asked; the profile is that same question, asked in writing.

s1.debrief: The Portal reads what you declare. The whole game is what you have written down, which is exactly where section two goes.
s1.watchFor: Questions about launch dates and feature details. Park them visibly: today is the preview and the readiness; launch specifics come from the program team.
s1.transition: So the matching runs on your profile. Time to build one worth matching.
s1.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; take answers to the ask question in chat.

s2.title: Getting findable
s2.purpose: Get every person to draft a full skills entry and a specific named interest before the Portal launches.
s2.say: Matching engines are honest machines: they can only see what you wrote. A profile that copies your job description makes you findable for the job you already have. The skills sweep and the named interest make you findable for the work you want next. And the skills your current role never uses are exactly where the interesting matches come from.
facilitate: Run Build your findability; two minutes for both choices, then run it.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: full inventory with evidence, one specific direction.

ask.q: Why do people leave the interest field blank?
expect: Fear of seeming disloyal or restless
Honestly not knowing what they want yet
ask.respond: That first fear is exactly what section three retires. For the second: name whatever is true this year. A draft interest beats a blank every time.

s2.debrief: Findable is a choice: every usable skill with evidence, one specific direction. Blank fields match nothing.
s2.watchFor: People underclaiming, especially long-tenured staff writing only current duties. Push the question: what can you do that this role never asks for?
s2.transition: Profiles ready. One thing left: believing it is safe to use them.
s2.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

s3.title: Moving is normal
s3.purpose: Retire the loyalty myths and state internal mobility as a normal, encouraged Vanderbilt career path.
s3.say: None of the tooling matters if people believe using it is dangerous. So hear it stated plainly: internal mobility is a normal, encouraged career path at Vanderbilt. A move across the university keeps your talent, your relationships, and your institutional knowledge here. The alternative to an internal move is usually an external one, and everybody loses that trade.
facilitate: Run Myth or normal? live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After round one, pause: ask who has heard that myth somewhere, show of hands or chat.
Run the breakout on what people have heard about applying internally.

ask.q: What would make you hesitate to use the Portal, honestly?
ask.respond: Name each one back to the room. The manager fear is the myth we just retired; the qualification fear is why matching runs on skills, never titles.

s3.debrief: Myths punish ambition, and they only survive in silence. Vanderbilt is saying the opposite out loud: move, grow, stay.
s3.watchFor: Anyone hearing this as a promise of promotions. The commitment is visibility of opportunity and safety to pursue it, never a guaranteed yes.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then you build your findability card.
s3.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the ask question.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now make it real. One skill or interest your title hides, in your own words. Pick the move, pick the window, build the card, and copy it somewhere you will see it before Friday. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitator.closeSay: You leave findable on paper; make it true this week. Thursday's Thrive Thursday takes the next step: advocacy, the difference between a mentor who gives you advice and a sponsor who spends their credibility on you. Being findable gets you surfaced; being sponsored gets you chosen. See you Thursday.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: Someone asks a launch-specific question the preview cannot answer
contingencies.then: Park it visibly: 'Good question, logging it for the program team.' Collect parked questions in chat and send them upward with the pulse; never guess at features.

contingencies.if: A participant says their manager punishes people for looking internally
contingencies.then: Take it seriously and keep it roles-only: 'If that is happening, there are channels for it, and I will point you to them after.' Restate the policy plainly; never litigate a specific manager on the call.

toughQuestions.q: Will my manager be notified if I update my profile or get matched?
toughQuestions.a: Your profile is yours, and keeping it current is normal professional upkeep, expected of everyone this month. Best practice is to bring your named interest to your manager yourself; a manager who knows your direction can advocate for it.

toughQuestions.q: Is this just a way to move people into jobs nobody wants?
toughQuestions.a: The matching starts from your skills and your named interests, and you can always say no. Surfacing is an offer; nothing about the Portal drafts anyone anywhere.

toughQuestions.q: I have been in the same role for fifteen years. Is this really for me?
toughQuestions.a: Especially for you. Long tenure usually means a deep skill set and a thin profile. The skills sweep is where fifteen years of capability finally gets written down, and stretch projects surface for exactly that depth.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Tuesday, 45 minutes on the Transfer Portal. A first look at how internal opportunities will start finding you. Bring nothing but an open question: what do I want next? Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did the findability move happen? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did the move on your card happen? 2) What did you claim that your title never showed? 3) What direction did you name?
